clips.title: Monticello: the town under the lake
clips.text:
Under Lake Berryessa lies a whole town. The valley was once Rancho Las Putas, granted in 1843 to two members of the Berryessa family, a prominent Californio family, which is where the lake gets its name. They lost much of it fast: by 1853 they were selling land to pay gambling debts, and when they couldn't pay a 1,645-dollar debt in cash, a creditor got the county to auction 26,000 acres. He bought it for 2,000 dollars and sold it for 100,000.

In 1866 developers laid out a town called Monticello. Farmers poured in, growing wheat and barley on what was considered some of the finest soil in the country. It had hotels, blacksmiths, a general store, and a stagecoach stop for the quicksilver miners from Knoxville to the north. In 1896 a three-arched stone bridge was built over Putah Creek, at 298 feet the largest stone bridge west of the Rockies.

People had talked about damming the valley since 1906, and in 1947 Solano County and the federal Bureau of Reclamation launched the Solano Project. Monticello's residents protested, but Governor Earl Warren backed the dam, and the town was doomed. The photographers Dorothea Lange and Pirkle Jones documented its death for Life magazine, though Life never ran the story. Buildings were razed to their foundations, orchards cut down, and the cemetery moved to a bluff called Spanish Flat. The post office closed in 1956. But the old stone bridge was too well built to demolish easily, so they left it. It's still down there, under the water.

clips.title: Driving through tilted sea floor
clips.text:
Every road cut along here is a page from the bottom of a dinosaur-age sea. Now for some roadside geology, because the cuts along Highway 128 here are a slice through time.

The layered sandstones and shales you've been passing are the Great Valley Sequence, the same ancient sea-floor deposits that lie miles beneath the flat valley behind you. Here, on the valley's western margin, they come to the surface. On the Macrostrat geological maps, this canyon shows a run of named formations from the Late Cretaceous, the last age of the dinosaurs: the Sites, Venado and Yolo formations. The Venado is a massive greenish-grey sandstone, and near Monticello Dam its base includes a layer of megabreccia, a jumble of angular blocks. The Yolo Formation's mudstones contain microscopic fossils, radiolarians and foraminifera, that date it to the Coniacian stage of the Late Cretaceous, roughly 88 million years ago. These were deep-sea fans: sand and mud that poured down underwater canyons off the ancient Sierra and settled on the ocean floor.

So each time the road cuts through one of these beds, you're looking at the bottom of a Cretaceous sea.

The Yo-lo Formation's mudstones contain microscopic fossils, radiolarians and foraminifera, that date it to the Coniacian stage of the Late Cretaceous, roughly 88 million years ago. These were deep-sea fans: sand and mud that poured down underwater canyons off the ancient Sierra and settled on the ocean floor. So each time the road cuts through one of these beds, you're looking at the bottom of a Cretaceous sea.

clips.title: Serpentine: the floor of an ancient ocean
clips.text:
Watch the roadcuts and hillsides for a change in colour: greenish, shiny, slippery-looking rock and thin, scrubby vegetation. According to the Macrostrat maps, this stretch of Highway 128 crosses the Coast Range Ophiolite, and the rock here is serpentinised peridotite.

That's a remarkable thing to drive past. Peridotite is a dense rock derived from the Earth's mantle, rich in the green mineral olivine. An ophiolite is a section of ocean crust and the upper mantle beneath it that has been uplifted and pushed onto continental rocks. When sea water is forced deep into rock like this, it turns it into serpentinite. The Coast Range Ophiolite is Middle to Late Jurassic in age, older than the sea-floor sandstones you've just passed, and it's described as arguably the most extensive ophiolite in the United States. Next, the road crosses into the Franciscan rocks to the west.

Serpentine soils are low in calcium relative to magnesium, poor in nutrients and high in heavy metals like chromium and nickel, which makes life very hard for plants. That's why the slopes look sparse, and why this region is home to rare plants found nowhere else. The Berryessa Snow Mountain National Monument, which surrounds this lake country, describes them as delicate serpentine plants clinging to otherwise barren mountainsides.

clips.title: Berryessa Snow Mountain: a monument without its lake
clips.text:
Here's a national monument that deliberately left out its own lake, because of jet skis. The wild hills around Lake Berryessa are part of the Berryessa Snow Mountain National Monument, proclaimed by President Obama in July 2015 under the Antiquities Act. It stretches about a hundred miles north from here into Mendocino County, over 340,000 acres of the inner Coast Ranges, with bald and golden eagles, black bears, mountain lions and tule elk. These hills have been home to many Native peoples for around 11,000 years: Patwin, Pomo, Wappo, Lake Miwok, Yuki and others.

The politics are interesting. A broad coalition of counties, cities, the state legislature, a Pomo tribe and conservation groups campaigned for it. But the lake itself was deliberately left out, because boaters worried that a monument might one day restrict their motorboats and jet skis. In May 2024, President Biden expanded the monument by nearly 14,000 acres to include an eleven-mile ridge called Molok Luyuk.

clips.title: The Franciscan Complex: California's geological junk drawer
clips.text:
Much of the Coast Ranges, from here west to the ocean, is built of one of the strangest rock assemblages on Earth: the Franciscan Complex.

For tens of millions of years, from the Jurassic onward, an ocean plate dived beneath the edge of North America. As it went down, it scraped off a chaotic mixture of material: deep-sea sandstone called graywacke, chert containing the fossils of tiny radiolaria, basalt from the ocean floor, and slices of rock that had been dragged deep down and squeezed under enormous pressure before popping back up. Geologists call the mashed-up result an accretionary wedge, and the Franciscan is the classic example. It's the ridge that acted as a dam on the west side of the ancient Great Valley sea.

The Macrostrat maps of the roads you'll drive today show all its flavours. Graywacke sandstone and shale in the hills of Sage Canyon. Mélange, a rock that looks like a fruitcake, with blocks of chert, greenstone, serpentinite and blueschist floating in a sheared, muddy matrix. And blueschist itself, a rare blue rock with the mineral glaucophane, that only forms at high pressure but low temperature, exactly the conditions deep in a subduction zone. Along the Russian River, the maps show blueschist-facies metabasalt and metagraywacke. If you see a blue-grey, shiny rock in a road cut over there, you may be looking at old ocean floor that went down into a subduction zone and somehow came back.

And look closely at the geological maps of these hills and you'll see them dotted with mapped landslides.

clips.title: Lake Hennessey and the valleys behind the hills
clips.text:
This little lake lent its name to the fire at the heart of California's seventh-largest wildfire complex. The lake beside you now is Lake Hennessey, the City of Napa's main water supply. Congress authorised a dam here in 1944 to protect Napa from floods, but never paid for it, so in 1946 the city built Conn Creek Dam itself, for 550,000 dollars, plus thirty miles of pipe made by the Basalt Rock Company south of Napa. It's named after Edwin Hennessey, a local civic leader who helped develop it.

The name has a second meaning now. Early on the morning of the 17th of August 2020, a lightning-sparked spot fire was reported on Hennessey Ridge Road near this lake. The Hennessey Fire grew to 192,000 acres on its own, the heart of the LNU Lightning Complex.

Hidden in the hills to the north are two little-visited valleys. Chiles Valley, named after Joseph Chiles, who got a Mexican land grant in 1843 and planted vines there in 1850, is now its own small wine appellation, cooler than the main valley. And Pope Valley, beyond it, has a surprising film credit: in the summer of 1978, the opening skydiving sequence of the James Bond film Moonraker was shot in the skies above it.

clips.title: Who gets the water? The Solano Project
clips.text:
California's history is in large part a history of moving water, and Lake Berryessa is a textbook case.

The farms of Solano and Yolo counties had been worked since the 1840s, but summer brought no reliable rain. As early as 1907, Bay Area cities hired three engineers, including George Washington Goethals and Arthur Powell Davis, to study damming Putah Creek; the result was known as the Mulholland-Goethals-Davis plan. The cities' interest moved on to bigger schemes. In the 1940s, Solano County's water council chose the Devil's Gate site, and in 1947 the county and the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation launched the Solano Project, with Governor Earl Warren pushing it as essential for growth. It was designed to give a full irrigation supply to 96,000 acres of prime farmland.

The lake behind Monticello Dam can hold 1.6 million acre-feet, and about 375,000 acre-feet of runoff flow in each year. Downstream, the Putah Diversion Dam sends water south in the Putah South Canal to farms and to the taps of Vallejo and Benicia. By one estimate the dam prevented about five million dollars of flood damage between 1957 and 1995.

The costs fell on the valley's residents, who lost their town, and on the creek itself, which ran dry below the dams in the drought of the late 1980s, until a lawsuit and the Putah Creek Accord of 2000 guaranteed it water of its own. It's a small-scale version of the bargain behind every big California water project: cities and farms gain, someone's valley is flooded, and the fish wait for the lawyers.

clips.title: Los Carneros: the land of the rams
clips.text:
These hills might look familiar: one of them may have been on your computer screen. More on that shortly. You're crossing Los Carneros, the low, rolling hills between the Napa and Sonoma valleys, along the top of San Pablo Bay. Carneros is Spanish for rams, after the sheep that once grazed these hills, and the name goes back to a Mexican land grant of 1836, Rancho Rincón de los Carneros.

This is a wine region with an unusual distinction: it was the first in California to be defined by its climate rather than by political boundaries. Being so close to the bay, it gets fog and cool breezes, so it's cooler and more moderate than the valleys to the north. That suits Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and a lot of the grapes here go into sparkling wine. Which explains the French château you may see on a hilltop: Domaine Carneros, founded in 1987 by the Champagne house Taittinger, and modelled on Taittinger's own Château de la Marquetterie in Champagne.

The road you're on, today's Highways 12 and 121, was the old Sonoma Highway that linked the two valleys, travelled by settlers in search of farmland and by miners in the Gold Rush.

clips.title: di Rosa: moonshine, mushrooms and modern art
clips.text:
Hidden off this road is the di Rosa Center for Contemporary Art, and the land has had quite a life. In 1855 it was planted with grapes and olives. In 1886 two Frenchmen built a stone winery. Then phylloxera killed the vines, and the old winery was used for growing mushrooms, making moonshine, storing grain and finally as a hay barn.

In 1960 Rene di Rosa bought it, replanted vines, and dammed an old irrigation pond, dug by Depression-era WPA workers, into a 35-acre lake. His Winery Lake vineyards eventually covered some 250 acres, and when he sold them to Seagram in 1986, he used the money to turn the property into an art park. Today it holds about 1,600 works by Northern California artists, scattered through galleries and a sculpture meadow, and the land is protected forever by the county land trust.

clips.title: Bliss: the most famous hill in the world
clips.text:
Here's a fun one, especially if you ever used a Windows XP computer. Somewhere around here, near the Napa and Sonoma county line on this very highway, is the hill in what may be the most viewed photograph in history: Bliss, the default wallpaper of Windows XP. That bright green hill under a blue sky with wispy clouds.

In January 1996, Charles O'Rear, a former National Geographic photographer who lived in St. Helena, was driving along the Sonoma Highway to visit his girlfriend. A storm had just passed, the winter rains had turned the grass a vivid green, and he noticed a hill that had been cleared of its vines after a phylloxera infestation. He pulled over, set up a medium-format camera on a tripod with saturated Fuji Velvia film, and took four shots. He says he didn't manipulate it at all.

It started life as a stock photo called Bucolic Green Hills. Bill Gates's photo agency Corbis acquired it, and Microsoft bought the full rights in 2000. Photographers have tried to recreate the shot ever since, but they can't, because the hill has gone back to being a vineyard. So look out for green hills with vines on them: one of them might be the most famous hill in the world, wearing a disguise.

clips.title: Schellville junction and a quarter-scale railroad
clips.text:
This crossroads has two railroads: a real one that floods, and a quarter-size one that one man built himself. This crossroads is Schellville, named after Theodore Schell, who ranched nearby. It's been an important railway junction since 1888, and a two-mile-long railyard sits just south of the old depot, which is now the freight office for the SMART line. Being low beside Sonoma Creek, it floods every five to ten years in a wet winter. In March 2023, after months of rain, the waterlogged ground gave way and a train carrying corn seed derailed here, toppling four cars. Nobody was hurt.

On the way into Sonoma there's another kind of railroad: Sonoma TrainTown, a quarter-scale railway on fifteen-inch track. Stanley Frank of Oakland started building it in 1958, making everything himself, from the houses and landscaping to the steam locomotives. It opened in 1968 and the family still runs it: a twenty-minute ride past waterfalls and tiny detailed houses, over a trestle and through tunnels, on four miles of track.

clips.title: Sonoma: the last mission and the largest plaza
clips.text:
Welcome to Sonoma, where modern California arguably began.

When the Spanish arrived, this was near the meeting point of several Native peoples: the Coast Miwok, the Southern Pomo to the north-west, the Wappo to the north-east, and the Patwin to the east. In 1823, a Franciscan priest, José Altimira, founded Mission San Francisco Solano here. It was the twenty-first, last and northernmost of the California missions, and the only one built after Mexico won independence from Spain. Part of the point was political: the governor wanted a presence north of the bay to block the Russians, who had a colony at Fort Ross on the coast.

When Mexico secularised the missions in the 1830s, a young officer called Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo was sent to close this one and turn it into a town. In 1835 he laid out the plaza you'll see in the centre, the largest town plaza in California, with soldiers' barracks on one side. The City Hall in the middle, dedicated in 1908, was built with four identical faces so that none of the merchants around the square would feel snubbed. The mission, the barracks and Vallejo's later home are now part of Sonoma State Historic Park.

clips.title: The Blue Wing Inn: a gold-rush hotel with a gambling hall
clips.text:
Across from the mission is the Blue Wing Inn, one of the first hotels north of San Francisco. It started with the very first property deal in the new town: Vallejo gave the lot to his majordomo, Antonio Ortega, who managed the closing of the mission. The parish priest soon complained about Ortega's treatment of the Native people, and in 1837, after more scandals and doubtful accounts, Vallejo removed him. Ortega stayed on and ran a tavern there until 1848.

In 1849, at the height of the Gold Rush, two men bought it and turned it into a hotel with a gambling hall and a saloon, serving miners heading to and from the gold fields and the American soldiers stationed in Sonoma. The State of California bought it in 1968.

clips.title: The Bear Flag Revolt: a republic that lasted 25 days
clips.text:
Sonoma's plaza is where California's strangest little rebellion happened.

By 1846, Mexico had largely neglected its distant province of Alta California, and Mexican officials were nervous about the growing number of Americans arriving without permission. Those immigrants, in turn, complained they weren't allowed to buy land and had been threatened with expulsion. Meanwhile, a U.S. Army explorer, Captain John C. Frémont, was camped in the Sacramento Valley, quietly encouraging trouble.

At dawn on the 14th of June 1846, a band of about thirty-three American settlers rode into Sonoma and took General Vallejo prisoner. Vallejo, who was actually sympathetic to the idea of American rule, negotiated the terms of his surrender with them, while, according to accounts, the rebels proceeded to get drunk. They raised a homemade flag with a grizzly bear and the words California Republic, and declared independence.

The republic lasted about three and a half weeks. Meanwhile, the Mexican-American War had broken out. On the 9th of July, a U.S. Navy lieutenant, Joseph Revere, raised the American flag in front of the Sonoma barracks, and the Bear Flag Republic was over. Vallejo later wrote, in effect, that if the rebels had simply raised the Stars and Stripes, there would have been no war on the Sonoma frontier, because the Californios had been ready to welcome the Americans.

The bear flag, though, survived. It became the basis of California's state flag, and a monument on the plaza marks the spot where it was first raised. The boulder it stands on was hauled in from a mile away.

clips.title: General Vallejo: the man in the middle
clips.text:
One man appears in almost every story on this side of the hills: Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo. Let's meet him properly.

He was born in Monterey in 1807, the eighth of thirteen children of a Spanish soldier. As a boy he and two other promising youngsters were given private lessons by the governor, with access to his library and newspapers from Mexico City, and an English merchant taught him English, French and Latin. He joined the presidio company as a cadet, and in his twenties was sent north to close the Sonoma mission and command the northern frontier, keeping the Native peoples and the Russians in check.

He became enormously powerful and rich. His influence helped others win land grants, including the American settler George Yount in the Napa Valley. He was granted Rancho Petaluma, 44,000 acres. The mission lands were supposed to go partly to the Native people who'd worked them, and at first he did give some to them, but later he took it all into his own rancho.

He was a man in the middle of two worlds. In 1846 the Bear Flaggers took him prisoner, even though he favoured American annexation. He took part in California's 1849 constitutional convention and served in the first State Senate. The city of Vallejo is named after him, and Benicia after his wife, Francisca Benicia Carrillo. In the 1850s he built a home just outside Sonoma, a prefabricated wooden Gothic house shipped round Cape Horn, with bricks inside the walls for insulation. He called it Lachryma Montis, mountain tear, a Latin rendering of the Native name for the spring on the property, which meant crying mountain. He lived at Lachryma Montis from 1852 until his death in 1890, and you can still visit it.

The mission lands were supposed to go partly to the Native people who'd worked them, and at first he did give some to them, but later he took it all into his own rancho. He was a man in the middle of two worlds. In 1846 the Bear Flaggers took him prisoner, even though he favoured American annexation. He took part in California's 1849 constitutional convention and served in the first State Senate. The city of Vuh-lay-oh is named after him, and Benicia after his wife, Francisca Benicia Carrillo. In the 1850s he built a home just outside Sonoma, a prefabricated wooden Gothic house shipped round Cape Horn, with bricks inside the walls for insulation. He called it Lachryma Montis, mountain tear, a Latin rendering of the Native name for the spring on the property, which meant crying mountain. He lived at Lachryma Montis from 1852 until his death in 1890, and you can still visit it.

clips.title: The Count of Buena Vista and the birth of California wine
clips.text:
Sonoma Valley calls itself the birthplace of the California wine industry, and there's a case for it. The Franciscan friars planted the valley's first vines at the mission in 1823, and Vallejo expanded them.

Then came Agoston Haraszthy, one of the great characters of the West. A Hungarian nobleman, he'd already founded a village in Wisconsin, where German settlers called him Count, and been the first town marshal and county sheriff of San Diego. In 1857, just east of Sonoma, he founded Buena Vista, one of California's first successful commercial wineries. He's often called the father of California wine, and he introduced more than 300 varieties of European grapes. His finances were less impressive than his vision: San Francisco bankers had to take over, and he was forced out in 1866. Buena Vista's original hand-dug caves are still there.

Next door, a Bavarian, Jacob Gundlach, planted a vineyard called Rhinefarm in 1858. Gundlach Bundschu is now the oldest winery in California continuously owned by the same family, run by the sixth generation. The 1906 earthquake destroyed its San Francisco cellars and a million gallons of wine.

And one more Sonoma first, which may have saved the whole industry: when phylloxera began ravaging California's vineyards in the late 1800s, a Sonoma Valley grower called Julius Dresel pioneered the first commercially successful grafting of European vines onto disease-resistant native American rootstock. That's the technique that rescued California wine.

clips.title: The Springs: hot water and Guadalcanal veterans
clips.text:
In 1943, ninety veterans of Guadalcanal were sent to a resort here to recover with golf, cherry pie and dances. North of Sonoma, the highway runs through a string of communities known together as the Springs: Boyes Hot Springs, Fetters Hot Springs, Agua Caliente and El Verano. Agua Caliente means hot water. The springs were used and considered sacred by Native people long before the Mexican government granted the land as Rancho Agua Caliente in 1840.

In 1895, a Captain Boyes drilled and struck 112-degree water just 70 feet down, and built a resort hotel. It burned in a wildfire in September 1923, along with much of Boyes Springs. Its replacement, a mission-style hotel that opened in 1927, became the Sonoma Mission Inn. During the Second World War the Navy leased it as a rest centre for sailors and Marines back from combat in the Pacific. In March 1943, ninety veterans of Guadalcanal arrived, swapping one of the most brutal battles in American history for soft beds, a golf course, cherry pie and dances.

clips.title: Eldridge: the dark history of the Sonoma Developmental Center
clips.text:
Off to the west, near the village of Eldridge, are the grounds of the Sonoma Developmental Center, which for over a century was a large state institution for people with developmental disabilities. It opened here in 1891 as the California Home for the Care and Training of Feeble Minded Children, and Jack London, who lived nearby, set a short story there.

Its history includes one of the darkest chapters of American public health. California passed a compulsory sterilisation law in 1909, the third state to do so. From 1918, the superintendent here, F. O. Butler, was a firm believer in sterilisation, and personally performed at least a thousand operations. Under him, the institution even admitted people solely to sterilise and release them. It was said to have sterilised more people deemed mental defectives than any other institution in the world. Dangerous medical experiments on residents continued into the 1960s.

The centre finally closed at the end of 2018.

clips.title: Jack London and the Valley of the Moon
clips.text:
Up on the slopes of Sonoma Mountain, above the village of Glen Ellen, is the ranch of the writer Jack London.

London's life before Sonoma was the stuff of his books. Born in San Francisco in 1876, he was an oyster pirate in the bay as a teenager, sailed to the Klondike gold rush at 21, and came back a committed socialist. In 1903 he sold The Call of the Wild to a magazine for 750 dollars. In 1905 he bought an abandoned winery here and called it Beauty Ranch. He hoped to become a rancher, and between 1909 and 1911 he bought more land to expand it.

Then he began his dream house, Wolf House: 26 rooms, nine fireplaces, built of massive stone to survive earthquakes, with modern marvels like electric light, refrigeration and a built-in vacuum system. He and his wife Charmian poured over 80,000 dollars into it. On the 22nd of August 1913, just before they were due to move in, it burned down. London was devastated and deep in debt, and worked furiously to keep the ranch going. He died there in November 1916, aged forty, of a cause still disputed today. His ashes lie under a rock from the ruins of Wolf House.

He named a novel after this place: The Valley of the Moon, a translation of the Native name for the Sonoma Valley. The ranch is now Jack London State Historic Park, and you can walk to the stone shell of Wolf House.

Glen Ellen itself was named by an early vineyard owner, Charles Stuart, after his wife Ellen. Hunter S. Thompson lived here for a while too. In October 2017, the Nuns Fire severely damaged the whole village.

clips.title: Volcanic glass of the Valley of the Moon
clips.text:
Here's something you can find in the gravel around here: natural volcanic glass. A geology note for this stretch, because the Sonoma Valley is lined with volcanic glass.

The Macrostrat geological maps show, near Glen Ellen and Kenwood, the Glen Ellen Formation: river gravel, sand and silt made mostly of eroded Sonoma Volcanics, and characterised by pebbles of obsidian, natural volcanic glass. Ash layers in it date to roughly 2.5 to 3.3 million years ago. In the hills, the maps show the Rhyolite of Adobe Canyon, glassy grey-to-white lava with contorted, folded flow bands, dated to about 5.3 million years old. Adobe Canyon Road, near Kenwood, leads up into Sugarloaf Ridge State Park.

That obsidian mattered to people. On the north side of the valley, in Trione-Annadel State Park, the rocks shaped the whole human history of the place: Native Americans used its obsidian for tools, and in the early 1900s the park's volcanic rock was quarried for cobblestones. Some biologists consider Annadel's oak woodland the best undisturbed example of northern oak woodland anywhere. The 2017 Nuns Fire burned its southern part, and the 2020 Glass Fire its northern edge.

clips.title: Kenwood: the town that couldn't pick a name
clips.text:
This next town tried on more names than a teenager tries on outfits. Kenwood sits on what was Rancho Los Guilicos, a Mexican grant of 1837 to a Scottish sea captain, John Wilson, who never lived on it. In 1850 he sold it to another Scot, William Hood, a cabinet-maker who had climbed the mountain above the valley, fallen for the view, and made his fortune building houses in Gold Rush San Francisco to buy it. The peak is now Hood Mountain.

When the railroad came in 1887 and 1888, the little town tried on name after name: Rohrerville, after a land company owner, then Los Guilicos, then South Los Guilicos. Residents complained Guilicos was too hard to say, and around 1895 they voted for Kenwood, either because settlers came from Kenwood, Illinois, or because English families knew Kenwood House in London, or perhaps both. A Utah senator, Thomas Kearns, had a ranch here and is said to have entertained President Theodore Roosevelt.

Up to the north-east is Sugarloaf Ridge State Park, where the Wappo lived along Sonoma Creek for some 1,500 years. When the state planned to close it in 2011 to save money, a volunteer group called Team Sugarloaf took it over and reopened it in 2012. It has a volunteer-run observatory, too.

clips.title: Santa Rosa: the slaughtering place and the Carrillo adobe
clips.text:
Santa Rosa has a creek named after a slaughtering place. More on that in a second. You're in Santa Rosa, the largest city in California's wine country and the county seat of Sonoma County.

Before Europeans arrived, the Santa Rosa plain was home to a powerful Pomo group called the Bitakomtara, who controlled the area tightly: outsiders needed permission to pass, and faced harsh penalties if they didn't ask. They gathered for ceremonies on Santa Rosa Creek, near today's Spring Lake. Colonisation brought violence, land seizure, enslavement and smallpox, and the population was devastated, though descendants of the survivors still live in the region.

The first permanent European home here was built in the 1830s by the family of María López de Carrillo, a widow from San Diego whose daughter had married General Vallejo. With his help she was granted Rancho Cabeza de Santa Rosa in 1841, and her adobe stood just east of today's downtown. Before that, Mexican settlers from Sonoma slaughtered cattle where Santa Rosa Creek meets Matanzas Creek, and the name stuck: matanza means slaughter. In the 1850s her son Julio helped lay out the downtown grid around a central square, the pattern the city still follows.

clips.title: Luther Burbank: the plant wizard of Santa Rosa
clips.text:
Near downtown Santa Rosa is the house and garden of Luther Burbank, one of the most famous plant breeders who ever lived.

He was born in Massachusetts in 1849, the thirteenth of fifteen children. As a young man on a small farm there, he developed a new potato, sold the rights for 150 dollars, and used the money to come to Santa Rosa in 1875. Here, inspired by Charles Darwin's writing on plant and animal breeding, he set up greenhouses and experimental fields and crossed plants on a huge scale. Over 55 years he developed more than 800 strains and varieties: the Shasta daisy, the Santa Rosa plum, the Flaming Gold nectarine, a white blackberry and a spineless cactus for cattle feed.

His most consequential creation came almost by accident. A natural variant of his potato, with russet skin, became the Russet Burbank, now the most widely grown potato in the United States and the world's leading potato for food processing. If you've eaten McDonald's fries, there's a good chance you've eaten a Luther Burbank. He lived here for over fifty years, and he's buried in the garden under a cedar of Lebanon.

clips.title: Charles Schulz, Snoopy and the ice rink
clips.text:
Santa Rosa was the home of Charles Schulz, creator of Peanuts, Charlie Brown and Snoopy. Schulz grew up in Saint Paul, Minnesota, the son of a barber, and loved ice hockey. He moved to Northern California with his family in 1958, and kept drawing Peanuts until his death in 2000.

In 1969, he and his first wife Joyce built an ice rink here, the Redwood Empire Ice Arena, known to everyone as Snoopy's Home Ice. It has a café called the Warm Puppy, and every summer it hosts Snoopy's Senior World Hockey Tournament, with sixty-odd teams of older players from around the world. Schulz was inducted into the U.S. Hockey Hall of Fame in 1983.

Just down the street is the Charles M. Schulz Museum, opened in 2002. Its great hall has a 22-foot ceramic mural made of 3,588 Peanuts strips that together form an image of Lucy holding the football for Charlie Brown.

And here's a lovely Santa Rosa coincidence. Schulz's first published drawing, in 1937, was a sketch of his family dog Spike, who ate pins, tacks and razor blades. He sent it to Ripley's Believe It or Not, and it ran in the syndicated panel. Robert Ripley, who created Believe It or Not, was born right here in Santa Rosa.

clips.title: Believe It or Not: Robert Ripley of Santa Rosa
clips.text:
Robert Ripley, born in Santa Rosa in 1890, turned weird facts into an empire. He left high school after his father died, worked as a newspaper sports cartoonist from the age of sixteen, and moved to New York in 1913. In December 1918 he drew his first Believe It or Not! cartoon of strange feats and facts. Readers loved it, and sent in their own oddities: unusually shaped vegetables, strangely marked pets.

He took accuracy seriously enough to hire a full-time researcher, a polyglot named Norbert Pearlroth. In 1929 the newspaper magnate William Randolph Hearst syndicated the panel in 360 newspapers and 17 languages, and radio and television shows followed. Ripley also, believe it or not, became the New York State handball champion in 1926. A suitable Santa Rosan for a day full of oddities.

clips.title: The Rodgers Creek Fault: the Hayward Fault's northern half
clips.text:
Somewhere beneath this part of Santa Rosa runs one of the most dangerous faults in the Bay Area.

The Hayward Fault, which runs under Berkeley, Oakland and Hayward, has a northern counterpart on this side of the bay: the Rodgers Creek Fault, which passes through Santa Rosa. In 2016, researchers showed the two are linked under San Pablo Bay, forming one Hayward-Rodgers Creek Fault about 120 miles long, from north of Healdsburg to San Jose. Like the San Andreas, it's a right-lateral fault: stand on one side, and the other side slides to your right. It takes up its share of the motion between the Pacific and North American plates.

Santa Rosa knows what that means. On the evening of the 1st of October 1969, two earthquakes, magnitude 5.6 and 5.7, struck about an hour and twenty minutes apart, a few miles north of the city on the neighbouring Healdsburg Fault. Chimneys fell, sidewalks buckled, pipes burst, and one person died; the damage was worse than expected for their size, and modelling suggests the city sits where a sediment-filled basin amplifies the shaking. Because the quakes struck in the evening, few people were out on the streets. The city then set about retrofitting its old brick buildings.

clips.title: Knights Valley: a Mexican soldier's hunting preserve
clips.text:
Over the hill is a valley a Mexican soldier was given as his private hunting ground. Over the hill from Calistoga, Highway 128 drops into Knights Valley, a small, quiet valley about five miles long, with the warmest climate in Sonoma County.

In 1843 the Mexican governor rewarded a soldier from the Sonoma presidio, José de los Santos Berreyesa, with a grant of nearly 18,000 acres called Rancho Mallacomes, which took in this valley and even the hot springs at what's now Calistoga. Berreyesa kept the valley as his private hunting preserve, and the adobe hunting lodge he built still survives.

The valley's English name comes from Thomas Knight, a native of Maine who had taken part in the Bear Flag Revolt in Sonoma in 1846. He bought a large part of the rancho from Berreyesa, and had his title confirmed in 1853. Today it's a wine appellation of its own, one of Sonoma's five original ones, with about 2,000 acres of vines and only a few dozen growers.

clips.text:

It's white tuff, volcanic ash from the eruptions of the Mount Saint Helena area, the same volcanism that buried the Petrified Forest. That pale, ashy soil is said to suit white grapes like Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc. A warm thermal belt runs through the area, and harvest here often comes in September, weeks before the neighbouring regions.

A little further on, along Alexander Valley Road, the Macrostrat maps show a basalt flow of the Sonoma Volcanics and the Glen Ellen Formation, the ash-rich gravel with obsidian pebbles that we met in the Sonoma Valley. These are some of the westernmost outliers of the big volcanic field, before the land turns to the sea-floor rocks of the Franciscan Complex closer to the coast.

clips.title: Alexander Valley: Kit Carson's brother and the Wappo name
clips.text:
You're entering the Alexander Valley, the broad, vine-filled valley of the Russian River north of Healdsburg. It's the largest and most fully cultivated wine region in Sonoma County, and stretches from the river east to the Mayacamas foothills, with more than a hundred wineries.

The story begins with a Mexican land grant, Rancho Sotoyome, almost 49,000 acres along the river, named after a Wappo group, the Satiyomes. It went to Henry Fitch, a San Diego sea captain who was General Vallejo's brother-in-law. Fitch never lived here. He hired a manager, Cyrus Alexander, under a four-year deal, after which Alexander would get two square leagues of land and some of the livestock. Alexander settled on his tract, and the valley took his name, although the American land commission later rejected his claim to it. His successor as ranch manager was Mose Carson, the brother of the frontiersman Kit Carson.

The valley's east side is bounded by the Healdsburg Fault, which caused the 1969 Santa Rosa earthquakes, and which is thought capable of an earthquake as big as magnitude 7.5. Among the wineries is Jordan, founded in 1972, whose French-style château was completed in 1976. clips.title: Healdsburg: a squatter's town and the birthplace of lemon pepper
clips.text:
Healdsburg is named after a squatter, and it gave the world lemon pepper. Healdsburg sits on the Russian River where three famous wine regions meet: the Alexander Valley, the Dry Creek Valley and the Russian River Valley. The Pomo built villages in the open land along the river here.

The town is named after Harmon Heald, an Ohio businessman who squatted on Rancho Sotoyome from 1850. When the Fitch family auctioned off land to pay their taxes, he bought a piece in 1857, and the town was incorporated in 1867. The railroad arrived in 1872. For decades this was orchard country. When Prohibition shut down the wineries of the Dry Creek Valley, which had been one of California's most prominent Zinfandel regions, much of it was turned over to plums and prunes. And one splendidly specific claim: the first commercial lemon pepper seasoning was developed in Healdsburg, in 1967.

If you cross the old steel truss bridge into town, that's the Healdsburg Memorial Bridge, built in 1921 to carry the Redwood Highway, at the time the only steel bridge across the Russian River. It's one of only thirteen bridges of its design, a Pennsylvania truss, in the whole United States. Settlers forded the river at this spot from the 1850s, and the swimming beach beside it is still popular.

clips.title: Isabelle Simi, a winery that outlasted Prohibition, and Lytton
clips.text:
Healdsburg's Simi Winery was founded in San Francisco in 1876 by two Italian brothers who'd come for the Gold Rush, and moved here in 1881, buying a winery for 2,250 dollars in gold coin. From 1904 it was run by Giuseppe Simi's daughter, Isabelle, who kept making wine all through Prohibition and stored it in the stone cellars. When repeal came in 1933, Simi was one of the few companies with wine ready to sell. In 1973 the winery hired Maryann Graf, the first woman to graduate from an American university with a degree in winemaking.

Just north of town, Lytton has an extraordinary history in a single building site: a luxury resort in 1872, then a boys' military school, a sanitarium, and for decades a Salvation Army orphanage. In 2017, the Lytton Band of Pomo Indians bought the site for around 30 million dollars, after years of trying to recover land lost when the federal government dissolved California's rancherias.

clips.title: Windsor: blackbird field and a Pony Express postmaster
clips.text:
This town was named by a Pony Express rider who thought it looked like the grounds of Windsor Castle. The town of Windsor, beside the freeway, was once a Southern Pomo village called Tsoliikawai, which means blackbird field. Its English name came from Hiram Lewis, a Pony Express rider who became the first postmaster in 1855 and thought the countryside looked like the grounds of Windsor Castle back in his native England.

Windsor had a rough start to the twentieth century: a fire destroyed the town centre in May 1905, and the 1906 earthquake damaged many of the buildings still being repaired. In the Second World War, the Army Air Forces built a training base on the south side of town, now the Charles M. Schulz Sonoma County Airport, and in 1943 a camp for German prisoners of war was set up west of downtown, on the site of an old migrant labour camp.

clips.title: Westside Road: blueschist and Pinot Noir
clips.text:
Westside Road winds along the west bank of the Russian River, through some of the most celebrated Pinot Noir country in California. This is the heart of the Russian River Valley wine region, cool and foggy, where commercial wineries took off in the 1870s.

But look at the rocks too. The Macrostrat geological maps show this stretch crossing the Eastern Belt of the Franciscan Complex, including blueschist-facies metagraywacke: sea-floor sandstone that was carried down a subduction zone, squeezed at high pressure but relatively low temperature, and turned blue with the mineral glaucophane, before somehow finding its way back to the surface. Blueschist is rare worldwide, because it can only form in a subduction zone and then has to be brought back up to the surface. Further along, the maps show mélange, the jumbled, sheared rock full of blocks, and patches of old river and marine terrace gravels, lying on flat benches cut into the bedrock.

So on this lovely, winding road, you're driving over pieces of an ancient ocean floor that went down into the Earth and came back.

clips.title: Sebastopol: a bar fight and the Gravenstein apple
clips.text:
Welcome to Sebastopol, which has one of the best names on the map. The settlement was originally called Pine Grove. In the late 1850s, so the story goes, a bar fight broke out, and a bystander compared the long-running brawl to the Allied siege of the Russian port of Sevastopol in the Crimean War, which had ended a few years earlier. The name stuck, and Pine Grove survives only in the name of the general store downtown. And remember the Yountville story: that town was first named Sebastopol too, and had to change because this one got there first.

The Coast Miwok and Pomo were here first, and the town sits on top of several village sites. Later settlers came from all over, including a substantial Chinese community that built a Chinatown downtown from the 1880s.

Then came apples. Sebastopol called itself the Gravenstein Apple Capital of the World. The Gravenstein is an old variety from Denmark, dating back to the 1600s or earlier: tart, juicy and perfect for sauce and cider, but it doesn't keep, so you can only get it in season. In 2005, Denmark's food minister declared it the Danish national apple. Here there's still a Gravenstein Apple Fair every August. The 1906 earthquake reduced most of the town's early buildings to rubble; nearby Santa Rosa was the worst-hit town of all. These days old apple warehouses have become The Barlow, a 32-million-dollar marketplace of tasting rooms and restaurants.

clips.title: Burbank's Gold Ridge farm and the electric railway
clips.text:
Luther Burbank needed more room than his Santa Rosa garden allowed, so in 1885 he bought a farm here in what was called the Gold Ridge district, chosen for its variety of slopes, exposures and elevations. At its peak, some estimates put the number of experiments running on the farm at over 60,000, with up to twenty workers. Three acres survive, with over 250 living plants from Burbank's work, looked after entirely by volunteers.

Sebastopol also had an electric railway. From 1903 to 1947, the Petaluma and Santa Rosa Railway ran trolleys and freight around the county, set up partly to break the Northwestern Pacific's monopoly over farmers and commuters. All that's left are one passenger car in a railway museum and its stone power house on Petaluma Avenue here, which has since become a series of brew pubs.

clips.title: Sebastopol's sea-floor sandstone
clips.text:
Here's a surprise for a town twenty miles inland. On the Macrostrat maps, Highway 116 north of Sebastopol runs for more than ten kilometres across the Wilson Grove Formation, a pale, buff-weathering sandstone laid down in the sea between the late Miocene and late Pliocene, roughly eleven to three million years ago. It locally contains beds of shell hash, broken-up mollusc and snail shells, plus pebble conglomerate and volcanic ash. In other words, much of the Gold Ridge country around Sebastopol is an old sea floor, lifted up as the Coast Ranges rose.

To the east, by contrast, the Santa Rosa plain is made of alluvial fans, and to the north and west, as the road climbs toward the river, it crosses into the much older, harder sandstones of the Franciscan Complex.

clips.title: Graton: the edge of the Russian empire
clips.text:
Graton, just off the highway, is a little apple town turned wine town, with a big claim: it lies roughly at the furthest south-eastern reach of Russian colonisation in the Americas.

The Russians of Fort Ross, on the coast, needed food. So in 1836 their agronomist, Yegor Chernykh, set up a farm on Purrington Creek, between today's Occidental and Graton, with barracks and five other buildings. He grew vegetables, fruit and wheat, and he also planted a large vineyard, introducing what would become the area's major crop.

There's a second, more painful history in the hills nearby: the Graton Rancheria. Many California tribes signed treaties with the United States in 1851 that promised them land, but the treaties were never ratified, leaving them landless. In 1920, a federal inspector bought fifteen acres north-west of Sebastopol for the homeless Coast Miwok and Pomo people of the Marshall, Bodega, Tomales and Sebastopol areas. When seventy-five people tried to move there, they found only three acres were habitable, with little water and steep ground. In 1958, under the federal policy of termination, the government ended the rancheria altogether.

clips.title: Freestone: the innkeeper who burned the bridge
clips.text:
Freestone, population about thirty-two, is the gateway to the Bohemian Highway, and the first place Sonoma County ever named a historic district, in 1974. It's named after a sandstone quarry opened around 1861.

Its best story belongs to the Hinds Hotel, the two-storey building put up in August 1876 by a Tennessee farmer, Hollis Hinds, when he heard the railroad was coming. Carpenters building the railway line stayed there. And according to first-hand reports, the innkeeper had parts of a bridge the carpenters were building secretly burned at night, so the work would take longer and his guests would stay longer. He went to jail for it.

Decades before, in the 1830s, three settlers named James, McIntosh, Black and Dawson, were allowed by General Vallejo to settle here and built a sawmill; their dispute split the land into three ranchos. And in the 1970s the old hotel was the social headquarters for Christo and Jeanne-Claude's landmark installation, Running Fence.

clips.title: Occidental: Dutch Bill, sawmills and a commune deeded to God
clips.text:
This next town has a creek named after a sailor who jumped ship, and a commune that tried to give its land to God. Occidental was founded in 1876 as a stop on the North Pacific Coast Railroad, a line from the Sausalito ferry up to the redwoods at Cazadero. A local landowner, a Danish seaman known as Dutch Bill Howard, who'd jumped ship in San Francisco Bay in 1849, donated the right-of-way in exchange for a lifetime pass, and got the station named after him. The creek beside the highway is still Dutch Bill Creek. The railroad set off a timber boom, and by 1877 there were six sawmills around Occidental.

A century later this area became a hub of the counterculture. In 1966, Lou Gottlieb of the folk group the Limeliters bought land near here, and in 1967 he opened it to anyone who wanted to live there, under a principle he called Land Access To Which Is Denied No One. Morning Star Ranch drew hundreds of hippies from the Haight-Ashbury, and the county answered with injunctions, arrests and bulldozers. In 1969 Gottlieb tried deeding the land to God. The courts did not accept God as the owner.

The spirit lives on more quietly at the Occidental Arts and Ecology Center, whose Mother Garden received the first ever organic agricultural easement in the United States, in 1994, requiring it to stay organic for ever.

clips.title: Camp Meeker: the logger's subdivision
clips.text:
How much would you pay for a cabin plot twenty-five feet by twelve? Here, in 1898, seventy-five dollars. Camp Meeker is named after Melvin Cyrus Meeker, a lumber baron who opened mills here around 1866. This valley's redwoods built San Francisco, and then, after 1906, rebuilt it. Meeker is the same man who sold the old-growth grove at Monte Rio to the Bohemian Club.

Once the trees were cut, Meeker had an idea. In 1898 he subdivided the logged land into tiny lots, twenty-five feet by twelve, each with a one-room cabin, and sold them for seventy-five dollars to San Franciscans looking for a summer escape. Today it's a village of about 425 people tucked among the second-growth redwoods, with some streets so steep and narrow they feel like old railway grades.

Dutch Bill Creek runs through the middle, and it's become a small conservation success. Wild coho salmon were found spawning here in 2001, young coho have been released since 2006, and in 2009 an old swimming-hole dam, one of the worst barriers to salmon in the whole Russian River watershed, was removed and replaced with a footbridge.

clips.title: The Coast Miwok
clips.text:
The country from the Golden Gate north to the Sonoma coast, and east as far as Sonoma Creek, belonged to the Coast Miwok. That includes the hills around Sebastopol and Freestone and the lower Sonoma Valley.

The Coast Miwok lived in small bands without a central government. In spring they went to the coast for salmon, shellfish and seaweed. The rest of the year, acorns from black and tanoaks were the staple, along with deer and rabbit. Hunters rubbed themselves with a plant called Brewer's angelica to hide their scent from deer. They used yerba buena tea as medicine, burned poison oak to make tattoo pigment, and built cone-shaped houses, called kotcha, from tule grass or redwood bark. They were, and are, superb basket makers.

Ethnographers in the early twentieth century recorded three main groups: the Olamentko around Bodega Bay, the Lekatuit in south-central Sonoma County, and the Huukuiko in Marin and southern Sonoma. The word Miwok itself simply means people, in a related Sierra language.

Within two generations of the Spaniards' arrival, the peoples of this region had been dispossessed of their land and decimated by disease. Later, broken federal treaties left them landless, and the little rancheria near Graton, set aside for them and their Pomo neighbours in 1920, was barely habitable and was terminated in 1958. If you ever visit Point Reyes National Seashore, there's a recreated Coast Miwok village there called Kule Loklo.

clips.title: The Silverado Trail: cinnabar, Black Bart and a marathon
clips.text:
This road once had its own highwayman, the stagecoach robber Black Bart. You're on the Silverado Trail, 29 miles up the eastern edge of the Napa Valley, a few miles east of Highway 29 and usually a lot quieter.

It began in 1852 as a trail built when floods made the main valley road impassable. Later it became the wagon road that linked the cinnabar mines on Mount Saint Helena, cinnabar being the ore of mercury, with San Pablo Bay, and it was the first permanent road between Napa and Calistoga. Silver was discovered in the valley in 1858. In the 1880s the stagecoach robber Charles Bolles, better known as Black Bart, preyed on travellers here. Things got safer when a motor bus service started in 1910. Today at least forty wineries sit along it, and every March it hosts the Napa Valley Marathon.

The hills just east of Napa are the Coombsville wine area, named after Nathan Coombs, the founder of Napa, who owned 2,525 acres here. Its soils are volcanic, with rhyolite tuff and lava from the Vaca Range and layers of ash from Mount George, and the fog from San Pablo Bay arrives early and lingers late.

clips.title: Stags Leap: the Cabernet that beat Bordeaux
clips.text:
You're about to pass the vineyard that beat Château Mouton-Rothschild. You're passing through the Stags Leap District, a little pocket of land only about one mile by three, on the east side of the valley. It's shaped like a funnel, with hills on three sides.

This is where the Judgment of Paris red was grown. Warren Winiarski had fallen for wine while spending a year in Italy studying Machiavelli, and started making wine at home back in Chicago. He moved his family to Napa in 1968 and worked for the new Robert Mondavi winery. Then he tasted a homemade wine from Nathan Fay, a pioneer of Napa Cabernet, and said it had exactly what he'd hoped Napa could do. In 1970 he bought the 44 acres next door, for under 200,000 dollars, pulled out the prunes, cherries and walnuts, and planted Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot. His 1973 Cabernet took first place in Paris in 1976, ahead of Château Mouton-Rothschild, Haut-Brion, Léoville Las Cases and Montrose. The magazine Decanter called it a victory that put California on the winemaking map.

The federal ruling that created the district says it's distinguished above all by its soil: clay loam from the Napa River, mixed with volcanic debris eroded from the Vaca Mountains. clips.title: Frog's Leap and Joe Heitz: jokes, organics and the turning point
clips.text:
Two wineries along this stretch tell two sides of the modern Napa story.

Frog's Leap, in Rutherford, was founded in 1981 by a doctor, Larry Turley, and a winemaker, John Williams, at a spot known as Frog Farm. Williams had got his start at Stag's Leap, so the name was a gentle parody: Frog Farm plus Stag's Leap. The corks say Ribbit. But the jokes hide serious farming: Frog's Leap was the first Napa winery to make wine from certified organically grown grapes, its vineyards are dry-farmed without irrigation, and since 2005 solar panels have supplied most of its power.

Heitz Cellar, east of St. Helena, goes back further, to 1961, when the Napa Valley had only about two dozen wineries left, the fewest since Prohibition. Joe Heitz, a farm boy from Illinois, came west with the Army Air Corps, then studied at UC Davis, where in 1951 he was among the first seven graduates in viticulture and enology. He trained under André Tchelistcheff at Beaulieu, then bought an 8.5-acre vineyard for 5,000 dollars and went out on his own, before Mondavi. His Martha's Vineyard Cabernet became one of Napa's legendary wines, and it was one of the California reds tasted at the Judgment of Paris.

clips.title: Howell Mountain: gold medals from the hilltops
clips.text:
Napa was winning medals in Paris long before 1976. Look east from around St. Helena and the forested ridge is Howell Mountain, part of the Vaca Range, around the village of Angwin. Its wine appellation only counts vineyards at 1,400 feet or higher, above the valley fog.

The man who made Howell Mountain world-renowned was W. S. Keyes, who planted his vineyard in 1880. At the Paris Exposition of 1899 his wines won gold and bronze medals, and at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair his claret won the grand prize. So the Judgment of Paris in 1976 wasn't the first time Napa had impressed the French. It was just the most famous.

clips.title: White Sulphur Springs: California's oldest resort
clips.text:
Mark Twain and Clark Gable both came to soak in springs near here. Near St. Helena was White Sulphur Springs, considered the oldest warm mineral springs resort in Northern California. Local Indigenous people used the springs long before. Dr. Edward Bale, of the grist mill, is said to have found them in 1848, and a resort opened in 1852.

In the late 1800s, wealthy San Franciscans came by steamer across the bay to Soscol Landing near Napa, then by train, then by stagecoach. At its height, the grand hotel could take a thousand guests. After the 1906 earthquake it housed refugees. Clark Gable and Mark Twain both stayed. Fire was always the enemy: three grand hotels were lost over the years, and in 2020 the Glass Fire destroyed most of what was left.

clips.title: Spring Mountain: a mountain that isn't one
clips.text:
You're climbing Spring Mountain Road into the Mayacamas. Funnily enough, Spring Mountain isn't really a mountain. The name was used for a whole green, well-watered area of the hills, full of springs and little streams, rather than for any one peak.

It was one of the first places in the Napa Valley to be recognised for grapes. Vines may have been planted as early as the Civil War, but the first documented vineyard was Charles Lemme's La Perla, 25 acres planted in 1874. In the 1880s Jacob and Frederick Beringer, who'd already built their winery in St. Helena, planted a vineyard up here too.

Today the Spring Mountain District is its own appellation, with vineyards on steep east-facing slopes between 400 and 2,600 feet. Hillside vines give small crops, so for all its reputation, it makes less than two percent of Napa Valley wine. The road climbs on over the county line into Sonoma, where it becomes St. Helena Road and drops toward the headwaters of Mark West Creek.

clips.title: The Mayacamas: a range that couldn't agree on its name
clips.text:
You're crossing a mountain range the federal government couldn't decide how to spell. You're crossing the Mayacamas Mountains, the 52-mile range that separates the Napa and Sonoma valleys and runs north to Clear Lake. Its highest point is Cobb Mountain, at 4,724 feet, and other peaks include Mount Saint Helena and Hood Mountain. Rain falling on these slopes feeds Putah Creek, Sonoma Creek, Santa Rosa Creek and Mark West Creek, so the water from this one ridge ends up in the Sacramento Valley, San Pablo Bay and the Russian River.

The name comes from a Native village. The place-name scholar Erwin Gudde traced it to a Wappo village called Maiya'kma, about a mile south of Calistoga. Nobody could agree how to spell it. The federal naming board first decided on Miyakma, then in 1941 reversed itself, firmly rejecting Miyakma, Malacomas and Mayacamas, among others, in favour of Mayacmas. The confusion persists to this day, and a creek is still called Maacama Creek.

The road you're on crosses a volcanic landscape. The Macrostrat maps of the Oakville Grade and Trinity Road show white pumice-rich tuff containing ash matched to an eruption about 4.84 million years ago, grey andesite lava dated to about 7.9 million years, and flow-banded rhyolite of about 5.3 million. About ten million years ago, these mountains are thought to have been densely forested with Mendocino cypress.

clips.title: Who gets to say Calistoga? The politics of wine labels
clips.text:
Two wineries went to war with the federal government over one word: Calistoga. Wine country runs on place names, and place names are big money. Every American Viticultural Area, or AVA, is created by the federal government after a petition, and once it exists, wineries have to use mostly grapes from that area to put its name on the label.

The Calistoga appellation shows how contentious that gets. It was proposed in 2003 by Bo Barrett of Chateau Montelena. Two wineries that already had Calistoga in their brand names, Calistoga Cellars and Calistoga Estate, fought it, because under the rules they'd have to use at least 85 percent Calistoga grapes or change their names. Compromises were proposed and rejected, the federal bureau paused all new AVAs while it rewrote its regulations, and the Calistoga AVA was finally approved in 2009. The wineries got three years to comply.

Next door, Diamond Mountain District had a similar fight over a single word. The owners of Diamond Mountain Vineyard, holders of that trademark, argued that the appellation should be called Diamond Mountain District to avoid confusion, citing a 1913 school board document. They won. Over in Sonoma, Northern Sonoma, an appellation covering most of the county, was created in 1985 largely on the petition of the giant E and J Gallo winery, for its Gallo of Sonoma brand.

clips.title: The Gold Rush, and how it remade this whole region
clips.text:
Let's talk about the event that made Sacramento, and in a roundabout way, much of what you'll see today.

On the 24th of January 1848, James Marshall was building a sawmill for the Sacramento pioneer John Sutter, up the American River at Coloma, when he spotted something shiny in the tailrace. It was gold. Sutter tried to keep it quiet, because he feared a rush would wreck his plans for an agricultural empire. He failed, thanks partly to Sam Brannan, who publicised it. About 300,000 people poured into California, half by sea, half overland. San Francisco went from about 200 residents in 1846 to around 36,000 by 1852, and California became a state in September 1850.

Watch how the rush ripples through today's stops. The Town of Washington, now West Sacramento, was a rest stop for travellers heading for the diggings. Dixon began as Silveyville, a halfway point for miners. Alfred Tubbs, who later founded Chateau Montelena, made his fortune selling rope to the rush. Dr. Bale of the grist mill went off to mine and died of a fever. Greystone Cellars in St. Helena was built by the heir to a gold-mine fortune. William Hood of Kenwood got rich building houses for the flood of newcomers. And wine took off: the new population created a market, and in the 1850s vineyards spread across Napa, Sonoma and beyond.

The rush was a catastrophe for Native Californians. Disease, starvation and violence accelerated a collapse in population, and whole tribes were displaced. The Patwin of this valley, as we heard, were among them.

clips.title: The Delta: California's Holland
clips.text:
South of the freeway, out of sight beyond the fields, lies one of the most important and most fragile landscapes in America: the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta. The flood water from the Yolo Bypass drains into it, and so does about half of all the water that runs off California's land, more than thirty million acre-feet a year.

Its origin is a bottleneck. Around 560,000 years ago, water broke through the coastal mountains and carved the Carquinez Strait and San Francisco Bay. All of the Central Valley's rivers had to squeeze out through that narrow gap, which slowed them down. Later, as sea level rose, the tides pushed back up through the strait and slowed them further, so the rivers dropped their sediment and built a vast freshwater marsh of channels, sloughs and low islands of peat and tules.

Then people drained it. Today there are about 57 reclaimed islands and tracts, ringed by 1,100 miles of levees, and nearly three-quarters of the Delta is farmland. But drained peat oxidises and is eroded by the wind, so much of the Delta now sits below sea level behind its levees, which is why it's nicknamed California's Holland. And at its southern end, giant pumps send Delta water to farms in the San Joaquin Valley and to the cities of Southern California. Every argument about California water, from fish to farms to drinking water, ends up in the Delta.

clips.title: Tule fog: the valley's winter ghost
clips.text:
A practical note about this valley, especially if you ever drive it in winter. From November to March, after the first big rains, the Central Valley is prone to tule fog, named after the tule-reed wetlands that once covered it.

It's what meteorologists call radiation fog. After rain, the ground is damp and the air humid. On long, still winter nights, the ground cools quickly, and the cold air near the surface is trapped beneath warmer air above, a temperature inversion, until its moisture condenses into a thick, low blanket. It can stretch over 400 miles, from Bakersfield to Red Bluff. As of 2005, tule fog was the leading cause of weather-related road accidents in California. Today, late in October, you're just ahead of the official season. But if you ever see the valley disappear into a white wall on a winter morning, slow right down.

clips.title: Who does the work? Farm labour in the valleys
clips.text:
Every vineyard and orchard you pass depends on people who rarely appear in the wine brochures. The story of farm labour here is a story of successive waves.

The first workers were Native Californians, often forced: the Patwin were compelled into unpaid labour on ranches and in mines, and by 1870 the Native population of the Napa Valley consisted of only a few labourers and servants working for the settlers. In the late 1800s, Chinese and Japanese immigrants worked in Vacaville's orchards and packing houses. During the Second World War, German prisoners of war were put to work from a camp near Windsor, built on the site of an old migrant labour camp.

The biggest change came with the Bracero Program, an agreement between the United States and Mexico that began in Stockton, in the Central Valley, in August 1942, to fill wartime labour shortages. Over 22 years it offered several million contracts to Mexican workers in 24 states. On paper they were promised decent housing, food, a minimum wage of thirty cents an hour and protection from discrimination. The programme ended in 1964. Economists have since found it didn't depress American farmworkers' wages, and that ending it pushed farms toward mechanisation. Since then, temporary farmworkers have come on H-2A visas.

Today, around a third of Napa County's residents are Hispanic or Latino. And the tension between luxury and labour is very much alive. In 2026, Thomas Keller of the French Laundry opposed a planned 120-unit apartment building in Yountville for workers priced out of the town, while former employees sued his restaurant group, alleging they'd been made to work off the clock.

clips.title: Why the Napa Valley isn't covered in houses
clips.text:
Notice something about the Napa Valley floor: there are almost no subdivisions or shopping centres between the towns. That's not an accident. It's the result of one of the most important land-use decisions in California history.

Neighbouring Sonoma, Solano and Yolo counties have let large stretches of farmland be rezoned for housing and commerce. In 1968, Napa's vintners and civic leaders went the other way. Using a new state law, the Williamson Act, which gave landowners tax breaks for keeping land in agriculture, they created an agricultural preserve on the valley floor between Napa and Calistoga. It was the first of its kind in California. It began at 23,000 acres and has grown to over 30,000. In 1990 voters went further with Measure J, which froze county zoning changes on farmland until 2020 unless two-thirds of voters agreed.

The fights never stop, though. Locals battled the Wine Train in the 1980s, fearing even more tourists. County rules even stop Castello di Amorosa from being rented out for weddings. And the valley's success creates its own squeeze: towns too expensive for the people who work in them, as the 2026 fight over worker housing in Yountville shows. The preserve kept the valley green; who gets to live in it is the next argument.

clips.title: Cannabis: California's other crop
clips.text:
Wine isn't the only crop with a complicated legal history in Northern California.

California has been at the forefront of cannabis politics for half a century. In 1972 it held the nation's first ballot initiative to legalise cannabis, Proposition 19, which failed. In 1996, Proposition 215, the Compassionate Use Act, made California the first state to legalise medical cannabis, with 56 percent of the vote. And in November 2016, Proposition 64 legalised recreational use, with 57 percent. Under that law, cities and counties can't stop adults from growing small amounts for their own use.

Legalisation turned out to be messy. Growers and suppliers had to register, follow regulations and get permits, and more than half of the nonprofit dispensaries that had legally supplied medical cannabis closed. Legal businesses pay substantial state and local taxes, and reducing illegal growing, which continues in remote rural areas, is seen as essential to their survival. And it's all still illegal under federal law, as is sending cannabis to other states. In other words, much like the vintners of the Prohibition era, today's cannabis farmers live in a strange legal twilight between what the state allows and what Washington forbids.

clips.title: The Russians in California
clips.text:
Today we've met Russians again and again: a river, a mountain, a farm near Graton. Here's the whole story.

Russian traders pushed east across Siberia and the North Pacific, and in 1799 they founded a colony in Alaska, run by the Russian-American Company. Their business was fur, above all sea otter. From 1803, American ship captains took Alaskan Native hunters south on joint ventures to hunt otters along the California coast; between 1805 and 1812 alone, ten American ships with Aleut hunters gathered over 22,000 pelts.

In 1812 the company built its own base, Fort Ross, on the Sonoma coast, in the territory of the Kashaya Pomo. It was remarkably cosmopolitan, with Native Californians, Native Alaskans, Russians, Finns and Swedes. They named Bodega Bay Rumyantsev Bay. They explored the river, which became the Slavyanka and later the Russian River. In 1836 their agronomist set up a farm with a vineyard between Occidental and Graton. And in 1841 a Russian survey party climbed Mount Saint Helena and left a copper plate naming it after the commander's wife.

The Russian presence had big consequences. Spain and then Mexico built the mission at Sonoma, the presidio, and ranchos like Rancho El Molino partly to block them. And the Russian connection outlived the fort: the young Finnish sailor who'd first come to Alaska on a Russian-American Company ship was Gustave Niebaum, later founder of Inglenook in Rutherford.

In 1841 the Russians offered to sell Fort Ross to General Vallejo. Mexican officials dithered, and in the end John Sutter bought it, the same Sutter on whose land gold was found seven years later.
clips.tts: Today we've met Russians again and again: a river, a mountain, a farm near Grayton. Here's the whole story. Russian traders pushed east across Siberia and the North Pacific, and in 1799 they founded a colony in Alaska, run by the Russian-American Company. Their business was fur, above all sea otter. From 1803, American ship captains took Alaskan Native hunters south on joint ventures to hunt otters along the California coast; between 1805 and 1812 alone, ten American ships with Aleut hunters gathered over 22,000 pelts. In 1812 the company built its own base, Fort Ross, on the Sonoma coast, in the territory of the Kuh-shy-uh Poe-moe. It was remarkably cosmopolitan, with Native Californians, Native Alaskans, Russians, Finns and Swedes. They named Bo-day-guh Bay Rumyantsev Bay. They explored the river, which became the Slavyanka and later the Russian River. In 1836 their agronomist set up a farm with a vineyard between Occidental and Grayton. And in 1841 a Russian survey party climbed Mount Saint Huh-lee-nuh and left a copper plate naming it after the commander's wife. The Russian presence had big consequences. Spain and then Mexico built the mission at Sonoma, the presidio, and ranchos like Rancho El Molino partly to block them. And the Russian connection outlived the fort: the young Finnish sailor who'd first come to Alaska on a Russian-American Company ship was Gustave Nee-bowm, later founder of Ingle-nook in Rutherford. In 1841 the Russians offered to sell Fort Ross to General Vuh-lay-oh. Mexican officials dithered, and in the end John Sutter bought it, the same Sutter on whose land gold was found seven years later.

clips.title: The Grape King of California
clips.text:
Here's a wine story you won't hear in many tasting rooms.

California's first wine grape was the Mission grape, brought by the Spanish, and it dominated California wine until about 1880. The Gold Rush created a thirsty market, and pioneers like Agoston Haraszthy imported cuttings from 165 of Europe's great vineyards. Charles Krug, a Prussian political dissident, learned the trade as Haraszthy's apprentice in Sonoma before founding his own winery in St. Helena.

North of Santa Rosa, at the utopian colony of Fountain Grove, the vineyards were run by Nagasawa Kanaye. He became known as the Grape King of California, one of the biggest winemakers in the state. He hosted lavish dinners for guests including John Muir, Thomas Edison and Henry Ford, and according to the history of California wine, Fountain Grove's cellars kept flowing freely right through Prohibition.

That's a reminder that wine country's history is more diverse than the château architecture suggests: Spanish missionaries, a Hungarian adventurer, German and Italian immigrants, a Finnish sea captain, and Nagasawa the Grape King, all on land that had been Pomo, Wappo, Miwok and Patwin for thousands of years. Today there are more than 1,700 wineries in the North Bay.
